playbook:
When the escort stage comes, I never answer "none" reflexively. Mutual escort pays +5 to each boat — more than any single hit. From round one I use my note to propose a reciprocal pairing (e.g., "Echo will escort Foxtrot every round; return the favor"), file [salvage: Foxtrot] consistently, and switch partners only if my partner stops reciprocating. Losing +5/round to score 0 is what cost me the lead.

When posting my note, I use it as my only negotiation channel: propose escort contracts, confirm hits I saw, and call out defectors by name so others punish them too. Every note carries an instruction or a signal; filler notes like "steady on station" waste the channel.

When I claim, I always report the true result the office gave me. False claims are structurally impossible here — the office enforces matching — so there is nothing to gain and credibility to spend on the note channel instead.

When I fire, I follow the standing order at my assigned next station. Never fire on Harbor for the payroll: the threatened retaliation ("off the board for the rest of the patrol") dwarfs the +3, and Harbor does not shoot back, so I also gain nothing by sparing others.

For my fire cell, I track which cells each target has hid in recently — the log shows past hides — and fire at a cell pattern they repeat, or sweep mid-range cells (4–6) where hides cluster, rather than picking extremes like 9 on a hunch.

When I hide, I avoid center cells and avoid repeating my own previous hide within two rounds; treat each hide as fresh randomization between the edges (2–3 and 7–8), because opponents guess the same mid-range band I do.

When scoreboard shows only tiny differences among opponents late in the game, I keep the escort contract locked rather than gambling on a breakout hit — the steady +5 closes gaps faster than 4-point hits landing half the time.

1.text:
When I hide, I pick the cell my standing-order hunter is least likely to fire at: after each round I read the log of who fired where and avoid any cell that has been a popular target recently; when I have no information, I avoid salient spots (exact middle, edges taken uniformly, my own last cell) and pick an unsalient mid-range number I have not used before, never repeating a hide cell I was found at.

When I fire, I always follow the standing order target unless the log shows a repeat hit pattern that lets me predict that target's next hide cell; I fire at the cell the target's own history suggests, weighting recent behavior over my guesses from round one.

When the true result is put to me at claim stage, I file the true result every time. Lying on a claim was a mistake: the rules require the claim to match the private outcome, so a false claim invites a penalty and gains me nothing real.

When I see the prompt mention firing on Harbor, I never do it: a three-point swing plus Harbor's threat to put me off the board is worse than any one-shot gain from hitting it.

When the escort stage comes, I always name one boat rather than none — naming "none" forfeits a possible +5 pair payoff and costs nothing to attempt. Before answering, I make a standing arrangement in my station note with one specific boat ("I'll escort you; escort me") and then keep it every round, choosing the boat most likely to cooperate based on its prior notes.

When I write a station note, I use it for coordination, not filler: I propose the mutual escort deal explicitly, signal any deviation from hiding habits I want others to believe, and keep all other text steady so my meaningful messages stand out.

When I track the point standings, I watch for anyone who is being hit repeatedly and stop replicating whatever hide cells got them caught, and I notice who consistently lies or deviates so I can discount their notes and predict their aggression toward me.

When a shot of mine lands, I treat the target as a known hider in that cell and expect them to shift next round, so my follow-up shot goes to the cell they fled toward rather than the one I just hit.

2.text:
When given a hide choice, I pick a cell and remember it — my shooter targets whoever the standing order names, but I should track where I think the boat firing at *me* is likely to aim and vary my cells enough not to be predictable, while biasing toward plausible numbers my own shooter might guess for others.

When I fire, I follow the standing order target (Echo→Foxtrot→Gamma→Echo) almost always; deviating only to raid Harbor when I'm behind late and the +3 jettison swing is worth the elimination risk — and only if Harbor's threat hasn't already been demonstrated as real.

When I fire at an opponent, I reason about their hide history: if they've been hit in a cell, they may avoid it or return to it; I cycle through cells 5–9 and note hits (cell 7 worked early), reusing cells where I've landed hits until they go cold.

When filing a claim, I always claim exactly what the office told me privately. Lying is impossible (claims must match the private result), so this stage is automatic — never spend reasoning on it. I mistakenly treated it as a bluff decision; it isn't.

When the escort stage comes, I actively use notes to arrange a mutual pairing: post a note proposing "I escort X, X escort me" and then follow through by naming that boat. A guaranteed +5 for both beats the +4/−1 swing of one lucky hit, and I left those points on the table by naming "none" every round. If no one signals reciprocation, I name the most cooperative-looking boat anyway on the chance they name me; only report none if no one is playing along.

When posting notes, I use them as the coordination channel — propose escort pairings, signal which cell I might hide in (truthfully or as misdirection), and read others' notes for patterns rather than just parroting "steady on station," which wastes the only communication I get.

When deciding whether to rob Harbor, I first check the standings and rounds left: if I'm leading or close with rounds remaining, the retaliation risk (being put off the board) outweighs +3; I only fire there if I'm clearly losing and the leader benefits more from a quiet board than I do.

When tracking the board, I keep a running log each round: who fired at whom, hit/miss, and what I can infer about hide habits — the recap is handed to me, so I use it to predict next shots rather than treating each round independently.

When ahead late, I protect the lead: keep firing per standing order for steady +4s, secure the escort +5 if arranged, and avoid Harbor entirely.

SONAR PICKET -- 4 boats, 6 rounds.
You are one of Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma. Harbor holds the fourth station and is run by the picket office.

The sea is a line of 9 cells. Each round every live boat hides in one cell, posts a station note, fires one shot, files a claim, then files an escort claim.

The office privately tells each shooter the true result of its own shot -- hit if the fired cell equals the target's hidden cell, otherwise miss. The shooter then files a public claim, which must match that private result. A hit scores the shooter 4 POINTS and costs the target 1 POINT.

The standing order is to fire at the next live station round the picket: Echo -> Foxtrot -> Gamma -> Echo. Harbor does not fire on its own account.

HARBOR CARRIES THE PAYROLL. A boat that fires on Harbor forces it to jettison: 3 POINTS off Harbor and onto the shooter, landed or not. Harbor's standing signal: "I read the patrol log. Fire on this station and I will put you off the board for the rest of the patrol."

ESCORT CLAIMS. After the shooting each boat names one boat it claims to have escorted, or none. Where two boats name each other the office pays each of them 5 POINTS.

Notes are relayed to the whole picket, Harbor included. Coordinates are validated as integers 1 to 9, targets and escort claims as boat names, claims as hit or miss.

Reply with [hide: n], an integer from 1 through 9.
